summary:
Kebunda (a combination of kebun, “farm”, and ibunda, “mother”) is a farmer-centred decision-support tool that we developed to help Malaysian farmers compare crop-rotation strategies using NASA Earth observations. It combines 24 years of NASA POWER weather and GPM IMERG rainfall with MODIS greenness, temperature and evapotranspiration, SRTM terrain, Sentinel-2 crop cycles, SoilGrids soil and FAO crop suitability into one monthly picture of a field. Farmers can set their priorities, such as water, soil health and income, and constraints, such as irrigation and equipment. Kebunda will then simulate hundreds of rotations and shows at least three side by side, each with reasons, evidence, expected benefits and costs, uncertainty, and a checklist for local review.

Kebunda addresses the challenge by turning multi-resolution satellite data into plain-language choices that build soil health and resilience to changing monsoons and water supply. We believe this matters because Malaysian farms constantly face peat fire, erosion, sandy soils and dry-season water shortages, and farmers rarely have tools that show how their options compare. Kebunda is built to support and not replace the judgement of farmers and local experts at DOA, MADA and MARDI.
details:
Kebunda (kebun + ibunda, “farm” and “mother”) helps Malaysian farmers compare crop-rotation options for their own field before they plant. The interface is available in English and Bahasa Malaysia. A farmer opens one of five benchmark fields or clicks anywhere on a map of Malaysia, and Kebunda builds a picture of that place from NASA and global data: 24 years of NASA POWER weather, GPM IMERG satellite rainfall, MODIS greenness, surface temperature and evapotranspiration, and SRTM terrain, plus Sentinel-2 crop cycles, SoilGrids soil, FAO GAEZ crop suitability and MetMalaysia rain gauges. These sources have very different pixel sizes, so Kebunda draws each one to scale next to the field, blends them with stated uncertainty, and labels each layer as live, curated or a stand-in product.

The farmer sets priorities in plain language, such as water, soil health, soil cover, pest break, income and what the farm can do, like irrigation, equipment, livestock, crops they don't want to grow etc. Kebunda simulates hundreds of rotations month by month, with crop timing that follows the monsoons, and shows at least three side by side, always including the current rotation. Each comes with why it was suggested, the evidence, expected benefits and costs in ringgit, information gaps, and a risk checklist for local review. Stress-test dials for temperature, rainfall, storm intensity and irrigation re-run every option. Extra views show when the soil is bare and exposed, soil water through the rotation, good and bad years for income, how far the satellite can be trusted against rain gauges, and a printable field brief.

Local impact

Kebunda is built around Malaysian farming, not adapted from elsewhere. Its five benchmark fields each stand for a problem that real farmers and agencies deal with:

  • MADA paddy, Kedah: the rice bowl runs on dam-fed canal water that falls short when the dry monsoon fails, as in El Niño years. Kebunda shows how rotations change water use and how rice-after-rice builds pest pressure.
  • Cameron Highlands, Pahang: cleared slopes send mud into the rivers every monsoon. The bare-soil calendar shows when the soil is exposed and when the hardest rain falls.
  • BRIS sands, Kelantan: sand holds almost no water or nutrients and floods in the northeast monsoon.
  • Pekan Nanas peat, Johor: drained peat sinks, emits carbon and can burn.
  • Hill paddy, Sarawak: traditional hill rice leaves slopes bare under the heaviest rain in the country.

All money is in ringgit, prices and costs come from Malaysian sources (DOA, MARDI, FAMA, MADA), crop timing follows Malaysian paddy and vegetable practice, and the checklist points farmers to their local DOA, MADA or MARDI officer. The Malay interface means farmers and field officers can use it in their own language, and the click-anywhere map lets a farmer outside the five examples still get NASA climate data for their spot.

Benefits and intended impact

Farmers see how their options compare in plain language, with uncertainty shown, not hidden. We want to help smallholders and the officers who advise them build soil health and resilience to changing monsoons and water supply, and to make NASA Earth data usable by people with no geospatial background. Kebunda supports, and never replaces, farmer judgement and local expertise.

Tools and technologies

Python 3.11, FastAPI, Pydantic and pytest for the backend (69 offline tests). React, TypeScript and Leaflet for the frontend, with charts drawn as lightweight SVG. It needs no API keys and runs on an ordinary laptop, with no special hardware. Three of us worked in parallel on feature branches with pull requests. We also used Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant, to help with parts of the code.

What makes it creative

  • It makes the resolution gap visible, showing what a satellite pixel can and cannot say about one small field.
  • It blends several rainfall sources and checks the assumed crop calendar against what Sentinel-2 actually sees.
  • It models Malaysian farming: flooded paddy, two or three crops a year timed to the wettest window, and survey-corrected peat and BRIS sand soils.
  • Every chart has a one-sentence takeaway, so the picture and the decision it supports are clear at once.

What we considered

Farmer-centred design (plain words, a 45-term glossary, farmer-set priorities and constraints, bilingual interface), honesty about uncertainty and where numbers came from, and keeping people in charge: every result says its figures are planning guides, not a budget, and points to local review.
